name: Amaranth Pink
lede: Amaranth Pink is a soft purplish pink named for the amaranth flower family, and recorded twice over in Robert Ridgway's 1912 color atlas.

sections.title: A name in the library
sections.body:
Ridgway's 1912 nomenclature lists this hue on plate XII, hue 69, tone d, and again on plate XXVI, hue 71′, tone d, an unusual double entry in a single atlas [1]. Maerz and Paul's 1930 dictionary separately dates the name to 1905 on plate 49 and again to 1912 on plate 50, so the two systems do not agree on a single first date either [1]. The amaranth plant family, from the Greek *amarantos* (unfading), has lent its name to a cluster of library pinks and purples since the nineteenth century [4].

In the color graph, the nearest neighbor is [[carnation-pink]], 3.2 units away, with [[mallow-pink]], [[kobi]] and the plainer basic term [[pink]] all close behind, each about 3.5 units off [2]. The ISCC-NBS system of 1955 classes it as a deep purplish pink, in block 248 [1]. The hex #F19CBB is a screen approximation of the atlas plate, not a dye sample [1].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: At a looser match (ΔE 10), our archive finds this pink in only 3 of 23,781 paintings, as photographed [3]. The strongest is Henri Matisse's *Nymph and Satyr* (1908); the others are an 18th-century English portrait and a 19th-century American harbor scene [3]. The rarity reflects this hue's narrow, specific pastel range, not any claim about where such pinks were historically used [3]. All matches are computed on photographed, varnished canvases [3].
